claims.text: Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
A carefully parameterized MEAM or EAM interatomic potential can represent the relevant FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle behavior.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower effective melting temperatures than larger ones.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo surface-driven phase transformations earlier than larger ones.
The proposed initial nanoparticles are equiatomic FeCuCrCoNi.
FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles can be prepared by pulsed laser deposition or an analogous synthesis method.
The relevant nanoparticle sizes range from below 10 nm to tens of nanometers.
A thermal simulation range from approximately 298 K to above 900 K is suitable for observing high-temperature structural changes and melting behavior.
The simulations should be conducted in vacuum or a controlled environment without extrinsic mechanical stress.
Decreasing nanoparticle size increases the surface-to-volume ratio and the proportion of surface atoms.
A higher proportion of surface atoms makes smaller nanoparticles more susceptible to atomic diffusion and surface melting.
At elevated temperatures, undercoordinated surface atoms in smaller nanoparticles have enhanced mobility.
Enhanced surface-atom mobility reduces nanoparticle thermal stability and promotes surface melting and phase transformation.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles retain more bulk-like thermal stability and show higher melting temperatures and delayed phase changes.
Pronounced atomic diffusion can drive temperature-dependent surface-layer formation, phase separation, and melting in quinary HEA nanoparticles.
The accuracy of the selected interatomic potential limits the reliability of the predicted thermal response.
The timescale accessible to molecular dynamics may limit the simulated thermal behavior.
In situ electron-microscopy heating can monitor nanoparticle structural changes, surface-layer formation, and melting during heating.
The exact melting temperatures, phase-transformation thresholds, and balance of kinetic and thermodynamic effects are uncertain.
Absence of a reproducible trend toward lower melting or earlier transformation with decreasing particle size would falsify the hypothesis.
